what_it_says: Prideaux gives Aisha's age as six when betrothed and eight when the marriage was consummated, and explains the early marriage as the usual custom of hot countries where girls are ripe at that age.
context: Prideaux narrates the Prophet's marriages in his Life, drawing on Arabic and Latin sources. The sentence is his own comment, placed between the marriage narrative and his explanation of the Prophet's mismatched marriages. He is writing for English deists in the context of the Christian polemic on Islam.
limits: Read from the page image (printed p. 54) and checked against OCR. The age figures are the traditional Muslim figures, repeated by Prideaux; he does not offer independent evidence. His explanation is partly a defence of the custom, not a criticism of the marriage as such, so it is rated explicitness 3.
stance: own view (explains the age by custom; the age itself is reported from the hadith tradition)

what_it_says: Prideaux says Aisha was not yet twenty when the Prophet died and that the widowhood of his wives was a hard restraint; he concludes that the Prophet made his imposture serve his lust.
context: The paragraph argues that the Prophet's revelations served his own desires, and cites the widowhood of his wives (Aisha among the youngest) as an example. The point is about the wives' restraint, not about the marriage ceremony itself.
limits: Read from the page image. The age is 'not then full twenty' at 632 CE (not an exact age). The criticism is of the Prophet's lust, not explicitly of marrying a child. Prideaux's marginal reference points to Johannes Andreas c.7 and Richardi Confutatio c.12.
stance: own view (criticises the Prophet's lust, by reference to Aisha's youth)

what_it_says: Gagnier states that the Prophet married Aisha at Mecca when she was seven and consummated the marriage at Medina when she was nine, and that she was the only virgin among his wives.
context: Gagnier's entry lists the Prophet's wives in order of marriage. The Aisha entry gives her age at marriage and consummation as a plain fact, and adds that she was the only virgin among his wives, the source of her father's nickname 'father of the virgin'.
limits: Neutral narrative: no criticism of the age is made in this passage. It is a compilation from Arabic traditions; Gagnier does not say whether he accepts them. Read from the page image.
